text.title: Hierarchical Index Failure Modes
text.summary: Six ways a tiered index becomes the bill it was built to avoid. All are silent: answers stay correct while cost climbs, which is why each needs a declared number rather than a review.

failure.symptom: Lookups are expensive and nobody can point to why. The retrieved content is small and obviously relevant; the total is an order of magnitude larger.
failure.cause: Index tiers grew with the corpus and no ceiling was ever declared, so the growth was never reported by anything.
failure.prevention: Declare the ceiling against the median body. Measured here: a 30,000-token index read delivering a 3,300-token body — a 10:1 walk-to-destination ratio that had accumulated unremarked.

failure.symptom: The index grows faster than the corpus. Each new leaf adds several lines rather than one, and the entries read like a catalogue.
failure.cause: Entries carry a prose summary restating the leaf, so the same text is paid once at the index and again at the leaf.
failure.prevention: Cap the entry to a discriminator that answers "when would I open this rather than its neighbours". The full summary already lives in the leaf's metadata and does not belong in the map.

failure.symptom: Content exists on disk, was correctly written, and is never retrieved. It is usually found by a broken-link audit rather than by a user.
failure.cause: Fan-out multiplied by depth no longer reaches the corpus: leaves were added without a matching entry, or a shard left orphans behind.
failure.prevention: Check `f^d >= corpus_size` at build time and audit index-to-filesystem reachability in the same job. Unreachable content is invisible, so no amount of usage feedback surfaces it.

failure.symptom: An over-budget index is brought back under budget, and routing quality drops immediately afterwards: the retriever starts choosing plausible neighbours.
failure.cause: The response to the size trigger was to shorten or delete entries, which removed discrimination rather than cost.
failure.prevention: Split on the declared partition key behind a stub. Trimming trades a cost problem for a correctness problem and hides the trade in a diff that looks like cleanup.

failure.symptom: A substantial one-off summarisation bill, a tree that must be rebuilt on every corpus change, and a hierarchy that mirrors the directory structure that was already there.
failure.cause: The build pattern was chosen before checking for a natural partition key.
failure.prevention: Exclude free sharding first. Recursive summarisation is the cheap end of the built structures — 115,541 tokens against 654,673 on the same corpus — but sharding an existing nesting costs zero, and zero beats the cheap end.

failure.symptom: Session cost rises with turn count even when later turns do no retrieval. The first lookup of a session is disproportionately expensive.
failure.cause: A long-lived orchestrator read a whole index into its own context instead of delegating the walk, so the index is re-sent with every subsequent turn.
failure.prevention: Delegate the walk and take back leaf paths with one-line reasons. An index read into a persistent context is not paid once — it is paid once per turn for the rest of the session.
